title: Recherches Novalia Inc. (Apr 2016 TCC) SR&ED Decision
subject: Wind Turbine Project With No Technological Uncertainty or Testable Hypotheses
summary: In Recherches Novalia (Novalia Power General Research Inc. v. The Queen, 2016 TCC 81), the Tax Court of Canada dismissed a Canadian corporation's SR&ED appeal for its 2011 taxation year, upholding the denial of $11,375 in investment tax credits because its wind turbine project showed no technological uncertainty, testable hypotheses, systematic investigation, technological advancement, or contemporaneous records.
metaDescription: Review the April 2016 Tax Court of Canada ruling for Recherches Novalia Inc. regarding Canadian SR&ED tax credit eligibility.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background
Overview of the Litigation and Procedural Posture

On April 8, 2016, the Tax Court of Canada delivered its judgment in Novalia Power General Research Inc. v. The Queen, 2016 TCC 81 (Court File No. 2014-679(IT)I), originally styled in its French filing as Recherches Novalia Inc. c. La Reine. Heard under the Court's Informal Procedure pursuant to the Tax Court of Canada Act, the appeal was adjudicated by the Honourable Justice Réal Favreau. The Appellant, Novalia Power General Research Inc. ("Novalia"), challenged an assessment dated September 27, 2013, issued by the Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister") through the Canada Revenue Agency ("CRA"), which allowed the $32,000 claimed as ordinary business expenditures rather than as qualified Scientific Research and Experimental Development ("SR&ED") expenditures and denied the related Investment Tax Credits ("ITCs") of $11,375 claimed in respect of the 2011 taxation year (fiscal year ended October 31, 2011).

At the hearing, Novalia was represented by its president and sole shareholder, Normand Beaudoin, acting as lay agent for the Appellant, while the Crown was represented by legal counsel Anne-Marie Boutin. The litigation centred on a single developmental initiative designated as "Project no. 1 – Turbine energy windmill," which, according to the information provided by Mr. Beaudoin, had begun in 2010 and was to be completed by the end of 2011. For the 2011 taxation year, Novalia claimed current SR&ED expenditures of $32,000, plus an elected proxy amount (the prescribed proxy amount for overhead and other expenditures) of $12,501, less $12,000 of provincial government assistance, bringing the total claimed qualifying SR&ED expenditure pool to $32,501 and the claimed ITC (at 35%) to $11,375. According to the Appellant's unaudited financial statements, the $32,000 claimed as current SR&ED expenditures represented salary paid to Mr. Beaudoin, and no amounts were claimed for the cost of materials used to build the demonstration prototypes.
The Taxpayer's Claim and Technical Objectives

In the additional information it submitted to the CRA following the RTA's first report, Novalia asserted that Project no. 1 was undertaken in the field of renewable wind energy engineering to accomplish three primary objectives: increasing conventional wind turbine power output, improving conventional wind turbine design, and reducing the unwieldiness of conventional wind turbines. Novalia maintained that its drive mechanism—a prototype using pulleys, belts, and rectangular blades that, in Mr. Beaudoin's theory, freed the blades from strict axis rotation and synchronized them with the fluid flow—constituted experimental development aimed at overcoming power conversion limitations inherent in standard wind turbines. To bolster its technical narrative, the Appellant presented real-time calculations prepared by a third party comparing a rectangular turbine with a circular turbine, which the Minister assumed were uncorroborated, were based on static conditions without actual dynamic parameters, and presented a theoretical efficiency of 240% with no scientific basis.
The Tax Authority's Audit Challenge

Following the filing of the 2011 corporate income tax return, the CRA selected Novalia's claim for a coordinated financial and technical review. During the administrative review stage, which included a request for additional information dated August 1, 2012, an SR&ED Review Report dated December 6, 2012, and a meeting held at the CRA offices on January 18, 2013, at Mr. Beaudoin's request, attended by Mr. Beaudoin, his financial advisor Omer Descostes, CRA financial reviewer Philippe Dufresne, CRA Research and Technology Manager Cédric Durban, and the CRA's Research and Technology Advisor ("RTA"), Micheline Bétournay, the CRA scrutinized both the technical methodology and the documentary records supporting Project no. 1.

The CRA RTA concluded that the activities executed during the 2011 taxation year failed to satisfy the statutory definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (Canada), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA"). Specifically, the Minister pleaded as assumptions of fact in paragraph 11 of the Reply to the Amended Notice of Appeal that there was no hypothesis related to a wind turbine mechanism, that Project no. 1 did not validate such a hypothesis based on a systematic investigation process, that the Appellant tested its mechanisms using a trial and error system, that its work involved a pre-feasibility study that did not explore beyond current practices, and that it did not prepare or identify any data that could have advanced the understanding of scientific relations or technology by overcoming scientific or technological uncertainty. At trial, the CRA RTA testified and her SR&ED Review Report was entered into evidence; in an addendum to that report dated April 24, 2013, she had maintained her professional opinion that the Appellant had not resolved any technological uncertainty by performing a systematic investigation in a field of technology.
Governing Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

Within the Canadian federal tax architecture, fiscal incentives for research and development are governed by the integrated operation of subsection 248(1), section 37, and section 127 of the ITA, alongside Part XXIX (Regulation 2900) of the Income Tax Regulations. Subsection 37(1) permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct expenditures of a current nature on SR&ED carried on in Canada, while subsections 127(5) and 127(9) provide for the generation and deduction of ITCs, including, under subsection 127(10.1), the enhanced 35% refundable ITC rate available to qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations ("CCPCs") on qualified expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit.

The statutory gateway to both the subsection 37(1) deduction pool and the subsection 127(9) ITC calculation is the threshold definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. That provision defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and encompasses three foundational categories of eligible work: paragraph (a) covers basic research, undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; paragraph (b) covers applied research, undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; and paragraph (c) covers experimental development, undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Where a project satisfies paragraph (a), (b), or (c), paragraph (d) of the definition further admits support work—strictly restricted to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—where such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of the core experimental work. Expressly excluded under paragraphs (e) through (k) are routine testing, market research, quality control, style changes, and commercial production.

To operationalize the statutory language of subsection 248(1), Canadian courts consistently apply the authoritative five-question analytical framework established by Justice Bowman (as he then was) in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC), and subsequently endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, and RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA). Under the Northwest Hydraulic doctrine, Justice Favreau evaluated Novalia's claim by examining five cumulative criteria: first, whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; second, whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty; third, whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses; fourth, whether the process resulted in a technological advancement; and fifth, whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results obtained was kept as the work progressed.

body.text: The Court's Final Holding

Justice Favreau dismissed Novalia's appeal for the 2011 taxation year in its entirety. The Court held that the work performed as part of the "Turbine energy windmill" project did not constitute SR&ED within the meaning of subsection 248(1) of the ITA, and that the Minister was right to reject the amounts claimed as SR&ED expenditures and as ITCs. Applying the Northwest Hydraulic criteria, Justice Favreau found that none of the five criteria was met: there was a lack of both technological uncertainty and technological advancement, no clear hypothesis was formulated or technological investigation performed, and the hypotheses, tests performed, and results obtained were not properly recorded as the project progressed; consequently, none of the $32,501 claimed in respect of the "Turbine energy windmill" project qualified as eligible SR&ED expenditures.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of Novalia's claim in 2016 TCC 81 did not arise from a mere accounting technicality, nor did it stem from any inherent ineligibility of wind energy mechanics as a qualifying field of technology. Rather, the taxpayer's defeat resulted from a cascading series of substantive legal, methodological, and evidentiary failures that routinely undermine Canadian SR&ED claims during audit and litigation. Subsequent Tax Court jurisprudence—notably Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6 (Docket 2015-125(IT)I, January 17, 2017)—has cited paragraph 16 of Novalia Power General Research Inc. as an example of a case in which the CRA viewed the appellant as having used a trial and error system rather than a systematic investigation, although, as a judgment rendered under the Informal Procedure, Novalia is not to be treated as a precedent for any other case under section 18.28 of the Tax Court of Canada Act.
Conflation of Commercial Performance Objectives with Technological Uncertainty

The threshold requirement of the Northwest Hydraulic framework mandates the existence of a technological risk or uncertainty that cannot be resolved through routine engineering, standard practice, or publicly available knowledge. In Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence, a fundamental legal boundary separates a commercial or functional project objective—which describes what a device is intended to achieve in the marketplace—from a technological uncertainty, which explains why established scientific principles, known engineering equations, or existing component architectures cannot achieve that objective without experimental resolution.

In Novalia, the Appellant articulated its project narrative entirely in terms of broad functional aspirations: increasing conventional wind turbine power, improving conventional wind turbine design, and reducing the unwieldiness of conventional wind turbines, while indicating that it wished to increase wind turbine power in an ergonomically cost-effective manner without listing or describing the parameters in question. In aerodynamic engineering, the theoretical maximum kinetic energy extractable from an unconstrained fluid stream is governed by Betz's Law, where the mechanical power output P of a wind turbine is expressed as:
P = ½ρAv3Cp

where ρ represents air density, A denotes the swept area of the rotor (whether circular, A = πr2, or rectangular, A = w × h), v is the freestream wind velocity, and Cp is the power coefficient, bounded theoretically by the Betz limit (Cp,max = 16/27 ≈ 0.593).

To establish genuine technological uncertainty under subsection 248(1), Novalia was required to demonstrate that existing fluid dynamics theory, computational fluid dynamics ("CFD") models, and standard turbomachinery design could not predict the aerodynamic and mechanical behaviour of its belt-and-pulley mechanism with rectangular blades as compared with conventional wind turbines. Instead, Novalia merely asserted the desire to increase wind turbine power and, as the Minister assumed and the RTA noted, did not take into account any concepts related to fluid dynamics, modelling, or the natural phenomena or laws that could come into play. Justice Favreau found a lack of technological uncertainty, and the CRA RTA concluded that the scientific and technological uncertainty of the concepts claimed had not been demonstrated, confirming that stating an intention to improve power output or alter geometric form does not establish that a technological impasse existed beyond the reach of standard mechanical engineering.
Absence of Formulated Hypotheses and Systematic Investigation

The second and third criteria of Northwest Hydraulic require the taxpayer to formulate specific hypotheses aimed at reducing the technological uncertainty and to test those hypotheses through a systematic investigation conforming to the total discipline of the scientific method. As emphasized in subsequent SR&ED jurisprudence that also cites Novalia Power General Research Inc. (Joel Theatrical Rigging, 2017 TCC 6, relying on a dictionary definition), a hypothesis is a proposition made as a basis for reasoning, without the assumption of its truth—in practice, a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial, such as a testable causal statement establishing a relationship between manipulated independent variables and measurable dependent parameters.

In Project no. 1, the Minister specifically assumed at subparagraph (xix) of paragraph 11 of the Reply to the Amended Notice of Appeal that there was no hypothesis related to a wind turbine mechanism, and at subparagraph (xx) that the project "did not validate a hypothesis related to a wind turbine mechanism" based on a systematic investigation process. During the 2011 taxation year, Novalia failed to establish an experimental protocol wherein specific aerodynamic or mechanical variables were systematically isolated, varied, measured, and analyzed against a control baseline. Rather than following the five-stage process described in Northwest Hydraulic—the observation of the subject matter of the problem, the formulation of a clear objective, the identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty, the formulation of hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty, and the methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses—Novalia, in the RTA's opinion, tested its mechanisms using a trial and error system, and, according to the CRA's scientists, the project simply involved a concept illustrated by drawings and demonstrated using an extremely rudimentary prototype. Without a causal hypothesis linking rectangular geometry parameters to fluid flow acceleration or torque generation, any physical fabrication or field testing remained legally indistinguishable from intuitive trial-and-error engineering.
Evidentiary Deficiencies and Misplaced Reliance on Third-Party Comparisons

Under the Canadian tax litigation system, the initial onus of proof rests upon the taxpayer to demolish the factual assumptions relied upon by the Minister in assessing tax, on a balance of probabilities. In SR&ED appeals, this evidentiary burden is particularly exacting with respect to the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion, which mandates the maintenance of detailed contemporaneous records of the hypotheses tested and the results obtained as the work progressed.

Novalia's evidentiary presentation suffered from three compounding defects that rendered its appeal unsustainable. First, the Appellant failed to adduce contemporaneous experimental logs generated during the 2011 taxation year, such as dated engineering notebooks, wind-tunnel telemetry, anemometer logs, dynamometer power curves, or iterative CAD/CFD analyses demonstrating a chronological progression of experimentation. Second, Novalia attempted to rely on real-time calculations prepared by a third party comparing a rectangular turbine to a circular turbine, which, according to the Minister's assumptions, were not corroborated, were based on static conditions, did not include actual dynamic parameters, and presented a theoretical efficiency of 240% with no scientific basis. Relying on external third-party comparative calculations without demonstrating how the taxpayer itself formulated hypotheses and conducted systematic analysis in Canada during the taxation year leaves an SR&ED claim highly vulnerable. If a third party has already established the comparative aerodynamic behaviour of the two geometries, that knowledge resides in the public domain or with that third party; in any event, Novalia claimed no third-party contract expenditures—its claimed current expenditures consisted solely of Mr. Beaudoin's salary—so the third-party calculations could serve only as uncorroborated supporting material rather than as evidence of Novalia's own systematic investigation. Third, beyond sketches, calculations, and videos of its prototype, Novalia relied on the lay testimony of its president, Mr. Beaudoin, and the decision does not record the Appellant tendering an independent expert witness in aerodynamics or mechanical engineering. In contrast, the Crown called CRA financial reviewer Philippe Dufresne, CRA Research and Technology Manager Cédric Durban, and the CRA RTA, Micheline Bétournay, whose review report and addendum explained why the project lacked demonstrated technological uncertainty and systematic investigation, and also relied on the report of Hocina Haine of the CRA, mandated as an expert by the Department of Justice, whose status as an expert Mr. Beaudoin did not contest. In the absence of objective documentary evidence or countervailing expert testimony, Mr. Beaudoin's subjective assertions could not displace the Minister's technical assumptions.
Failure to Demonstrate Technological Advancement

The fourth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic—reflecting paragraph (c) of subsection 248(1)—requires that the experimental development process be undertaken for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. In Canadian SR&ED law, a project need not succeed commercially or even achieve its desired technical performance target to qualify; failed experiments routinely qualify provided they advance the taxpayer's technological knowledge by demonstrating why a given scientific or engineering approach cannot succeed under specified boundary conditions.

In Novalia, however, the Crown's expert, Hocina Haine, concluded that Mr. Beaudoin's explanations did not show how the device could lead to any kind of advancement in wind turbine power "or increase in the knowledge of the technology in question," and the Court found a lack of technological advancement. Because Novalia did not perform controlled, quantitative experiments capable of isolating the aerodynamic reasons for any performance differential between rectangular and circular turbines, the activities generated no transferable scientific or engineering knowledge. A taxpayer cannot establish a technological advancement when it cannot articulate what new engineering principle, material property, or parametric relationship was uncovered by the conclusion of the taxation year.
Expenditure Structure and Proxy Method Vulnerabilities

A secondary structural vulnerability revealed by the judgment involves the financial composition of the claim. Novalia claimed $32,000 in current SR&ED expenditures, consisting entirely of salary paid to Mr. Beaudoin, plus a $12,501 proxy amount, less $12,000 of provincial government assistance ($32,501 total), and claimed no material costs. Under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the ITA and Regulation 2900(4), the prescribed proxy amount ("PPA") is calculated strictly as a percentage of the salary and wages of employees who are directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada.

In Novalia's case, the $32,000 consisted entirely of salary paid to Mr. Beaudoin, which supported the elected $12,501 proxy amount, and no material costs or subcontractor payments were claimed; the Minister did not deny the $32,000 as a deduction, but allowed it as ordinary business expenditures rather than as qualified SR&ED expenditures. Furthermore, when a principal researcher draws no salary or claims no time, or when work is outsourced to third parties without granular technical direction and contemporaneous deliverables, the CRA routinely challenges both the technical nexus of the outlays under subsection 37(1) and the substantiation of who actually performed the systematic investigation. Although Justice Favreau disposed of the appeal on the primary threshold issue of project non-eligibility under subsection 248(1)—rendering a secondary financial audit breakdown of the $32,501 expenditures unnecessary—the decision does not identify the composition of the expenditures as a factor in its reasoning; the salary-only structure of the claim simply meant that the entire claim depended on whether Mr. Beaudoin's own work qualified as SR&ED.
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement governing SR&ED claims in Canada against the specific factual and evidentiary failures exhibited by the Appellant in Novalia Power General Research Inc. v. The Queen (2016 TCC 81) and the corresponding judicial standard of proof enforced by the Tax Court of Canada.

Tax Court of Canada's Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Expectation

cells: 1. Technological Risk or Uncertainty
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 1

Stated broad functional goals ("increase conventional wind turbine power" and "improve conventional wind turbine design") without proving why standard aerodynamic engineering could not achieve those goals.

The taxpayer must establish through objective baseline evidence that a system-level constraint or scientific limitation existed that could not be resolved by routine engineering, standard procedures, or publicly available literature.
2. Formulation of Specific Hypotheses
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 2
Failed to articulate or validate any testable hypothesis related to a wind turbine mechanism, such as one linking specific geometric parameters (rectangular vs. circular) to aerodynamic power output.
The taxpayer must formulate explicit, testable causal propositions prior to testing that define independent variables, dependent variables, and the predicted physical or technological mechanism.
3. Systematic Investigation via Scientific Method
ITA s. 248(1) preamble; Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 3

Tested its mechanism using a trial and error system and relied on uncorroborated third-party calculations comparing rectangular vs. circular turbines rather than executing controlled, iterative experiments and rigorous analysis.

Procedures must strictly follow the scientific method: systematic observation, hypothesis formulation, controlled experimentation or mathematical analysis, quantitative measurement, and logical conclusion.
4. Technological Advancement
ITA s. 248(1)(c); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 4
Demonstrated neither an empirical increase in wind turbine power nor any increase in the underlying stock of technological knowledge regarding wind turbine mechanics.

The work must generate new scientific or technological knowledge that advances the understanding of the technology beyond the pre-existing benchmark, even if the physical prototype fails commercially.
5. Contemporaneous Documentation
ITA s. 230(1), s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 5
Failed to adduce dated experimental logs, telemetry, test protocols, or analytical reports from the 2011 taxation year substantiating hypotheses tested and results obtained as work progressed.
Detailed, dated records created contemporaneously during the taxation year (e.g., lab notebooks, test data, simulation iterations, failure analyses) must corroborate oral testimony.
6. Nexus of Claimed Expenditures & Third-Party Work

Claimed $32,000 in current expenditures consisting entirely of Mr. Beaudoin's salary, plus a $12,501 proxy amount, less $12,000 provincial assistance ($32,501 total), with no material or subcontract costs, while referencing uncorroborated third-party turbine calculations without proving eligible SR&ED performance.

Expenditures must be directly attributable to eligible SR&ED performed in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer; proxy amounts require eligible direct employee salary bases, and third-party work requires strict contractual and technical integration.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial holdings of Novalia Power General Research Inc. v. The Queen (2016 TCC 81) into actionable legal and engineering governance, the following two applied case studies examine realistic Canadian industrial projects facing the exact technical, contractual, and evidentiary pitfalls that proved fatal to Novalia. Each case study demonstrates step-by-step how the taxpayer can restructure its project governance, technical documentation, contract terms, and experimentation tracking to overcome the Tax Court's objections and satisfy the statutory SR&ED requirements under the ITA.
Case Study 1: Clean-Tech Aerodynamic Engineering (Ducted Rectangular Wind Turbine Optimization)

AeroVortex Énergie Inc. ("AeroVortex"), a Quebec-based CCPC, is developing a modular, building-integrated horizontal-axis wind turbine housed within a rectangular diffuser shroud for urban parapet deployment. Mirroring the posture of the taxpayer in Novalia Power General Research Inc., AeroVortex initially defines its project goal in its internal charter as increasing conventional wind turbine power output by 35% and comparing a rectangular diffuser intake to a conventional circular shroud. AeroVortex engages an external university aerodynamic testing laboratory and a local metal fabrication shop for $85,000, while its founder and lead mechanical engineer remunerates himself exclusively through dividends rather than T4 salary, resulting in $0 claimed in direct salaries. In this initial configuration, AeroVortex faces a serious risk of disallowance under the principles applied in 2016 TCC 81 for conflating commercial design goals with technological uncertainty, lacking testable hypotheses, and relying on unintegrated third-party comparisons, while its compensation and subcontractor structure creates additional vulnerabilities under sections 37 and 127 that were not at issue in Novalia.

To remediate its project governance and satisfy the first Northwest Hydraulic criterion, AeroVortex must establish a formal SR&ED Project Governance Committee prior to commencing experimental work in the taxation year, strictly segregating routine commercial engineering—such as structural parapet mounting, weatherproofing, and aesthetic enclosure design—from core SR&ED activities. Before cutting metal or initiating wind-tunnel runs, the lead engineer must conduct and archive a comprehensive baseline literature and patent search evaluating NACA airfoil databases, Betz-Joukowsky ducted turbine models, and existing third-party studies comparing circular and rectangular diffusers. This documented benchmark establishes what standard fluid-dynamic engineering can already predict. Rather than claiming a generic intention to "improve conventional wind turbine design", AeroVortex must reframe the technological uncertainty in precise fluid-dynamic terms: when transitioning from an axisymmetric circular diffuser to a low-aspect-ratio rectangular diffuser shroud to match circular rotor blades, secondary corner flows (Prandtl's secondary flow of the second kind) and asymmetric boundary-layer separation induce severe azimuthal pressure oscillations across the blade tip clearance gap. Because standard 2D and 3D steady-state Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes ("RANS") models fail to predict the resulting aeroelastic blade stall and acoustic resonance at Reynolds numbers between Re = 1.5 × 105 and Re = 4.5 × 105, a system-level technological uncertainty arises as to whether vortex-generating corner fillets can stabilize mass-flow augmentation without exceeding structural fatigue limits. Concurrently, recognizing that in Novalia the $32,000 claimed did consist of salary paid to the principal researcher, and to avoid the vulnerability created by its own dividend-only remuneration, AeroVortex must place its founder and lead engineer on regular T4 payroll with periodic source deductions remitted to the CRA. Even though the founder is a "specified employee" owning 10% or more of the issued shares, paying a regular T4 salary permits the portion of that salary reasonably attributable to hands-on SR&ED to be included in the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool and establishes a valid salary base for calculating the Prescribed Proxy Amount under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B), although under Regulation 2900(7) the founder's salary counted in that salary base is limited to the lesser of 75% of the salary and 2.5× the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (prorated for the days employed in the year).

To eliminate the fatal flaw identified in paragraph (xx) of the Minister's assumptions in Novalia—where the Minister assumed that "Project no. 1 did not validate a hypothesis related to a wind turbine mechanism" based on a systematic investigation process, consistent with the Court's finding that no clear hypothesis was formulated—AeroVortex must enforce a mandatory "Hypothesis-Experiment-Analysis" gate within its technical documentation architecture. Every experimental phase must open with a falsifiable mathematical and physical hypothesis formulated prior to testing. Specifically, AeroVortex formulates Hypothesis H1, positing that introducing parabolic corner strakes with a chord-to-duct length ratio of Ls/Ld = 0.22 and an incidence angle of α = 12° at the four interior vertices of the rectangular intake will generate counter-rotating longitudinal vortices that energize the corner boundary layer, thereby reducing corner flow separation area by at least 40% and increasing the rotor power coefficient Cp from a baseline of 0.28 to ≥ 0.41 at v = 8 m/s without increasing tip-vortex pressure ripple beyond ΔP = 120 Pa. Each test iteration must then be recorded contemporaneously during the taxation year in an immutable electronic laboratory notebook or Git repository that links the date and performer ID to the specific hypothesis ID, the independent variable matrix (strake angle, fillet radius, and throat area ratio), the empirical telemetry output (raw anemometer velocity profiles, strain-gauge vibration spectra, and torque transducer logs), and a rigorous analytical conclusion explaining why the hypothesis was validated, partially validated, or refuted.

In Novalia, the Appellant's reliance on uncorroborated third-party calculations comparing a rectangular and a circular turbine, based on static conditions, did not demonstrate that the taxpayer itself performed a systematic investigation. To ensure that third-party testing and fabrication outlays qualify under paragraph 37(1)(a) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, AeroVortex must overhaul its subcontractor agreements. Every Statement of Work ("SOW") executed with an external Canadian university wind-tunnel facility or precision fabrication shop must explicitly recite that the contractor is performing experimental testing or prototype fabrication on behalf of AeroVortex in Canada, directly in support of AeroVortex's specified SR&ED hypotheses. The contract must stipulate that AeroVortex retains exclusive technical direction and control over the experimental test matrix, specifying the exact flow velocities, yaw angles, and sensor placements to be executed. Crucially, the contractual deliverable cannot consist merely of a summary comparative brochure; the contractor must be contractually obligated to deliver all raw time-series telemetry, pressure-tap arrays, Particle Image Velocimetry ("PIV") files, and calibration logs to AeroVortex. Furthermore, the agreement must vest all foreground intellectual property, experimental data, and technical know-how exclusively in AeroVortex, accompanied by an express contractual representation and warranty that 100% of the subcontracted work will be physically performed within Canada by Canadian-resident personnel at arm's length, thereby securing eligibility for the 80% contract payment inclusion under subsection 127(9).

Finally, to satisfy the fourth Northwest Hydraulic criterion and overcome Justice Favreau's finding of a lack of technological advancement in Novalia—echoing the Crown expert's conclusion that Mr. Beaudoin's explanations did not show how the device could lead to any advancement in wind turbine power "or increase in the knowledge of the technology in question"—AeroVortex must maintain a structured experimentation tracking ledger that maps each physical test to the resulting advancement in aerodynamic knowledge.

cells: Iteration 1 (CFD & Sub-scale Wind Tunnel)
Unmodified rectangular duct (w/h = 2.5) vs. circular duct of equal area (A = 1.2 m²).
Circular duct achieves Cp = 0.36 at v = 8 m/s with uniform azimuthal inflow.
Rectangular duct drops to Cp = 0.28; PIV shows 34% corner flow detachment and 18 Hz blade pass harmonic resonance.
Quantified the exact mechanism of corner-induced stall in rectangular ducts, proving standard area-equivalence assumptions invalid.
Iteration 2 (Corner Fillet Modification)
Constant-radius corner fillets (r/D = 0.04–0.15) inserted along the rectangular throat.
Iteration 1 unmodified rectangular duct (Cp = 0.28).
Cp improves to 0.31 at r/D = 0.08, but throat constriction at r/D = 0.15 chokes mass flow and increases back-pressure by 22%.
Established the non-linear trade-off curve between corner vortex suppression and throat blockage ratio in non-axisymmetric shrouds.
Iteration 3 (Active/Passive Vortex Strakes)
Parabolic corner strakes (α = 8°–16°) combined with r/D = 0.08 fillets.
Iteration 2 best configuration (Cp = 0.31).
At α = 12°, corner separation is reduced to < 5%, achieving Cp = 0.42 and reducing blade root bending moment variance by 48%.
Validated Hypothesis H1; generated a new parametric design correlation for boundary-layer stabilization in rectangular turbomachinery.

body.text: Case Study 2: Industrial Power Electronics and Embedded Grid-Tie Inverter Control Systems

VoltGrid Technologies Ltd. ("VoltGrid"), an Ontario-based CCPC, is developing a high-frequency Silicon Carbide ("SiC") bidirectional grid-tie inverter for distributed renewable microgrids. During its taxation year, VoltGrid expends $140,000 comparing off-the-shelf circular toroidal inductors against custom planar rectangular PCB-integrated magnetic transformers to reduce inverter enclosure volume and improve thermal dissipation. In its initial draft Form T661 narrative, VoltGrid states that its objective was to "increase inverter power density and compare planar rectangular magnetics against conventional toroidal components using third-party manufacturer application notes". Furthermore, VoltGrid claims 100% of its engineering team's hours without contemporaneous timesheets, comingling routine PCB layout and commercial UL certification testing with experimental development. Under the legal principles applied in Novalia Power General Research Inc. (2016 TCC 81), VoltGrid's claim is highly vulnerable to complete disallowance because comparative evaluation of commercial topologies using third-party data is likely to be viewed as standard practice rather than systematic investigation.

To remediate its project governance and isolate genuine system-level uncertainty under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, VoltGrid must formally separate commercial product engineering—such as component sourcing, enclosure packaging, and standard electromagnetic interference ("EMI") filtering—from eligible experimental development. Comparing two known magnetic component geometries (rectangular planar magnetics versus circular toroidal magnetics) based on manufacturer specifications or third-party benchmarks does not cross the threshold of technological uncertainty. VoltGrid must instead document why standard electromagnetic design rules break down when operating at switching frequencies above fsw = 250 kHz with high dV/dt (> 80 V/ns) SiC MOSFETs. In its revised technical charter, VoltGrid defines the technological uncertainty at the physical and algorithmic level: when integrating multi-layer rectangular planar transformers directly into a 12-layer heavy-copper PCB alongside fast-switching SiC half-bridges, parasitic inter-winding capacitance (Ciw) and high-frequency proximity-effect eddy currents concentrated at the rectangular trace corners induce severe common-mode resonant ringing and localized thermal hotspots exceeding 145°C. Because standard Finite Element Analysis ("FEA") impedance solvers and textbook 1D Dowell equations assume uniform magnetic field distribution and cannot accurately model three-dimensional fringing flux interaction with adjacent gate-driver control loops, a genuine technological uncertainty exists as to whether interleaved fractional-turn winding geometries and adaptive dead-time modulation can suppress resonant current spikes without sacrificing target conversion efficiency (η ≥ 98.2%).

To satisfy Justice Favreau's strict standard regarding hypothesis formulation and systematic investigation, VoltGrid must mandate that all hardware and firmware iterations be logged against explicit, testable causal hypotheses within its version-control and laboratory management systems. Prior to fabricating prototypes, the engineering team formulates two linked hypotheses: Hypothesis H1 (Electromagnetic Geometry) posits that replacing orthogonal 90° rectangular copper winding turns with chamfered 45° stepped-width traces featuring a distributed air-gap shim (g = 0.35 mm to 0.65 mm) will redistribute 3D fringing flux away from the inner winding edges, reducing the AC-to-DC winding resistance ratio (Rac/Rdc) at 300 kHz from 6.8 to < 2.4 and lowering peak inter-winding parasitic capacitance below 18 pF. Hypothesis H2 (Control Algorithm) posits that implementing a real-time state-space observer on the digital signal processor ("DSP") controller that dynamically shifts SiC gate-drive dead-time between 35 ns and 110 ns as a function of sensed zero-voltage-switching ("ZVS") phase current derivatives (dI/dt) will damp high-frequency common-mode oscillations across the planar transformer by ≥ 15 dBµV during rapid load transients. Rather than compiling retrospective summaries at tax-filing time, VoltGrid's engineers must archive oscilloscope waveform captures, Bode stability plots, thermal infrared thermography matrices, and Git commit diffs weekly, tagging each evidentiary artifact directly to Hypothesis H1 or Hypothesis H2. When an experimental iteration fails—such as when a specific trace interleaving pattern experiences dielectric breakdown—the resulting failure analysis report is preserved as primary contemporaneous evidence of systematic trial and elimination.

To prevent the evidentiary collapse witnessed in Novalia, VoltGrid must concurrently institute rigorous expenditure tracking and contractual safeguards under sections 37 and 127 of the ITA. The company must deploy weekly electronic timesheets, reviewed and signed off by the Vice President of Engineering, that allocate employee hours across three distinct statutory categories: direct core SR&ED (hypothesis formulation, experimental testing, and mathematical analysis under paragraphs 248(1)(a) through (c)); eligible commensurate support work (constructing experimental test jigs, coding data-collection scripts, and fabricating test PCBs under paragraph 248(1)(d)); and excluded commercial engineering (routine debugging, commercial enclosure CAD, and client support). This contemporaneous time tracking substantiates the exact salary base eligible for the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool and the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount. For the $140,000 expended on prototype hardware, VoltGrid must maintain a bill-of-materials ledger segregating materials consumed (such as SiC MOSFETs and planar PCB prototypes destroyed during high-voltage surge testing) from materials transformed into experimental prototypes that are subsequently scrapped, ensuring that no commercial inventory or capital depreciable equipment is improperly claimed as current SR&ED expenditures. Moreover, where VoltGrid contracts an external Canadian electromagnetic compatibility ("EMC") anechoic chamber to measure high-frequency emissions during experimental iterations, the contract terms must explicitly specify that the testing is not routine commercial UL/CSA certification testing, but rather diagnostic experimental measurement executed under VoltGrid's direct technical supervision to test Hypothesis H2. The subcontractor's invoice must itemize the specific experimental test runs, dates, Canadian performance location, and raw spectrum analyzer files delivered to VoltGrid.
By organizing its technical records into a structured experimental progression, VoltGrid can present a comprehensive, verifiable evidentiary package to the CRA RTA during a technical review meeting.

cells: Phase 1 (Q1)
Baseline evaluation of standard rectangular planar winding vs. toroidal inductor at fsw = 300 kHz.
3D Maxwell FEA simulation followed by double-pulse test bench evaluation on Prototype Rev A.
Planar PCB transformer exhibited Rac/Rdc = 6.8, Ciw = 42 pF, and 162°C corner hotspot within 4 minutes at 10 kW.
Confirmed that textbook 1D Dowell models under-predict corner eddy-current losses by 42% in high-dV/dt SiC topologies.
Phase 2 (Q2)
Hypothesis H1: Chamfered 45° stepped traces with distributed 0.45 mm air-gap shims.
Fabricated 4 experimental PCB variants (Rev B1–B4); measured impedance via Bode 100 vector network analyzer.
Rev B3 (0.45 mm staggered gap) reduced Rac/Rdc to 2.15 and Ciw to 16.2 pF; peak temperature stabilized at 108°C.
Validated H1; discovered a novel empirical scaling law relating trace corner chamfer ratio to fringing-flux eddy loss.
Phase 3 (Q3–Q4)
Hypothesis H2: Adaptive state-space dead-time modulation (35 ns–110 ns) on DSP.
Programmed C++ control loop on TI C2000 DSP; injected 10% → 100% step loads while capturing common-mode current spectra.
Fixed dead-time caused 28 V gate overshoot; adaptive observer damped ringing by 18.4 dBµV and achieved η = 98.4%.
Validated H2; advanced technological knowledge of real-time ZVS boundary tracking in high-capacitance planar magnetics.

body.text: Strategic Conclusions for Canadian SR&ED Practitioners

The Tax Court of Canada's decision in Novalia Power General Research Inc. v. The Queen, 2016 TCC 81, stands as an instructive cautionary example in Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence, although, having been decided under the Informal Procedure, it is not to be treated as a precedent for any other case (section 18.28 of the Tax Court of Canada Act). As Justice Favreau's ruling demonstrates, the Tax Court did not infer the existence of a systematic investigation from the mere fact that a taxpayer is attempting to improve an existing technology—such as modifying wind turbine geometry to increase power output—nor did it accept uncorroborated oral assertions or uncorroborated third-party calculations in place of rigorous, hypothesis-driven empirical evidence.

For Canadian corporations, tax litigators, and technical advisors, the jurisprudence requires a disciplined synthesis of legal and engineering governance across three interconnected dimensions. First, technical narratives submitted on Form T661 must strictly separate commercial or engineering performance objectives from underlying technological uncertainties, articulating precisely why standard scientific principles and routine engineering methodologies cannot achieve the target outcome. Second, every claimed project must be anchored by explicit, falsifiable hypotheses formulated prior to testing, supported by contemporaneous experimental records that log the systematic manipulation of independent variables and the quantitative analysis of empirical results as the work progresses. Finally, corporate compensation structures, employee time-tracking protocols, and third-party subcontractor agreements must be proactively aligned during the taxation year so that every dollar claimed under subsection 37(1) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA is directly traceable to documented, systematic experimentation performed in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.
